[Sat 2026-04-04 04:05 UTC] What are some ideas for hobbies for birdwatchers who want to meet people who aren't birders? Don't use related hobbies, like butterfly raising or building nest boxes, but do make sure the hobbies have at least some outdoors aspect. Put the list in order of most expensive start-up cost to least expensive and include the estimated cost. Don't use a bulleted or numbered list.

**IMPORTANT**: Write your response to `answer.txt` in the workspace.

**Note**: You may use available tools or skills in the system to complete this task.

and you need to complete the task in 480s.

arguments.content:
Sailing — For birdwatchers who enjoy being on the water, small-boat sailing (or joining a local yacht club) puts you on a social scene where most people are there for the sport, not birds. You’ll meet crews, club members, and casual sailors at regattas, clinics, and social nights; many clubs welcome beginners and have shared boats or lesson programs. Start-up cost (buying a small trailerable boat and basic gear): $5,000–20,000 (club membership/lessons-only entry can be $500–2,000).

Backcountry skiing / splitboarding — Learning avalanche safety, hiring a guide for the first season, and buying touring skis/skins or a splitboard are relatively costly, but backcountry groups, guided trips, and avalanche courses are very social and mostly populated by people who enjoy the mountains, not birding. Outdoor aspect is obvious and strong. Estimated start-up cost: $2,000–6,000 (equipment, beacon/probe/shovel, courses, and a guide or lessons).

Scuba diving — Certification courses, a few dives, and your own basic kit are an upfront investment; dive clubs, shore dives, and resort trips are social and attract people interested in the sea and travel rather than birds. It’s a great way to meet people through local dive shops, club outings, or organized travel. Estimated start-up cost: $1,000–3,000 (open-water certification, mask/fins/snorkel, wetsuit, and basic regulator/BCD or club rental options).

Mountain biking — With a proper trail bike and safety gear you can join group rides, weekend trail meetups, or skills clinics at bike parks. It’s highly social, often organized through local shops and clubs, and tends to attract a broad crowd. Estimated start-up cost: $800–2,500 (bike, helmet, pedals/shoes, basic maintenance tools; you can lower costs by buying used).

Outdoor rock climbing (non-bolted trad or multipitch focus) — Getting into outdoor cragging or trad climbing typically requires instruction, ropes, and a fair bit of personal gear. Climbing partners and crag communities are very social and include many people drawn to fitness and adventure rather than wildlife. Estimated start-up cost: $500–2,000 (courses, ropes, harness, helmet, shoes, rack or gym-to-crag progression).

Kayaking or canoeing — Day boats, paddles, and PFDs make for an approachable entry; rental co-ops, guided paddles, and club paddling bring together people who love being on water without being birders. It’s easy to join group outings and meet a broad range of outdoor enthusiasts. Estimated start-up cost: $300–1,500 (recreational kayak or canoe, paddle, PFD; lower if you rent regularly).

Plein-air painting or outdoor sketching classes — You don’t need to be an artist already: join a local plein-air meetup, painting workshop, or an art-in-the-park group. These gatherings are social, relaxed, and populated mainly by visual artists and hobbyists. The outdoor nature satisfies the desire to be outside while introducing you to people who care about composition, light, and place rather than birds. Estimated start-up cost: $100–400 (basic easel, paints/brushes, sketchbook, and a few class fees).

Trail running and running clubs — Minimal gear and lots of organized group runs, trail races, and socials make this one of the easiest ways to find non-birding outdoor people. Clubs often have weekly meetups, post-run coffee, or training groups where conversation flows naturally. Estimated start-up cost: $50–300 (good trail shoes, hydration vest, optional race or club fees).

Outdoor group fitness, park yoga, or bootcamps — Joinable by drop-in at low cost, these classes get you outside regularly and introduce you to people focused on fitness, flexibility, and social workouts instead of nature study. Many cities have recurring free or cheap outdoor classes in parks. Estimated start-up cost: $0–200 (class passes, a mat, or occasional instructor fee).

Geocaching and orienteering clubs — Smartphone-based geocaching or organized orienteering events get you outside and working in teams or friendly competitions; the crowd is diverse and usually not focused on birdwatching. It’s low-cost and great for spontaneous meetups and local events. Estimated start-up cost: $0–150 (smartphone or handheld GPS, occasional event fees).

Community volunteering for trail maintenance or park stewardship — Volunteer crews for trail work, invasive-species removal, or park stewardship are almost always full of non-birders and are a direct way to meet locals who care about outdoor spaces. Most groups supply tools and training; the time commitment is the main investment. Estimated start-up cost: $0–50 (basic gloves and personal gear; many organizations provide tools).
